name: How do analysis patterns differ from design patterns? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Analysis patterns work on the conceptual problem-domain model and can drive our questions when we clarify functional requirements.
answers.comment: L5, slide 4: They capture functional requirements on the problem-domain model without redrawing it again and again.

answers.body: Design patterns serve a maintainable decomposition of classes: attributes, methods, precise relationships and their collaboration.
answers.comment: L5, slide 4: Design patterns describe the static and dynamic structure and collaboration of the key participants in a software design.

answers.body: Analysis patterns prescribe the attributes, methods and precise class relationships that the final code will use, in programming-language terms.
answers.comment: L5, slide 4: Those are design-level details; analysis patterns stay with domain-level terms.

answers.body: Design patterns are mainly a tool to elicit use cases from stakeholders, which is why they use problem-domain terms.
answers.comment: L5, slide 4: Eliciting functional requirements is the role of analysis patterns, not of design patterns.

answers.body: Both kinds work with programming-language classes and differ mostly in how many classes a single pattern contains.
answers.comment: L5, slide 4: They differ in level and purpose, not in size: conceptual domain model versus design of classes.

name: Which statements correctly describe what a design pattern is and why teams use patterns?

answers.body: A pattern is a general reusable solution to a common problem; it is a meta-model that must be instantiated with design decisions.
answers.comment: L5, slide 5: A pattern is not a finished design, so compromises and consequences have to be weighed and patterns combined.

answers.body: A pattern name is a shared vocabulary: "here we use Observer" tells everybody how the objects collaborate.
answers.comment: L5, slide 5: Shared vocabulary means better communication, faster design and an improved team culture.

answers.body: A pattern is a finished design that can be copied into the system and needs no further decisions from the team.
answers.comment: L5, slide 5: The slide stresses that a pattern is not a finished design.

answers.body: Every design problem has exactly one matching pattern, so understanding the problem fully determines the pattern to use.
answers.comment: L5, slides 5-7: Applying a pattern to the wrong problem is a typical mistake; designers must judge between similar patterns.

answers.body: A pattern is a library class that is imported into the project and then extended by subclassing in each application.
answers.comment: L5, slide 5: A pattern is a description of a solution (a template), not a piece of reusable code.

name: Which of the following are typical mistakes or problems when designers use design patterns?

answers.body: Believing that the best design applies as many patterns as possible to the model.
answers.comment: L5, slide 7: This is named as a wrong premise; patterns have to solve actual problems.

answers.body: Solving every problem with the most recently learned pattern.
answers.comment: L5, slide 7: Applying a pattern to the wrong problem is a typical problem.

answers.body: Choosing between patterns by their class diagrams alone, although many patterns look alike.
answers.comment: L5, slide 7: Strategy and State look alike, so the designer must understand all aspects of the patterns.

answers.body: Reading the Consequences of a pattern carefully before deciding to use it in the design.
answers.comment: L5, slide 9: Consequences are critical for evaluating design alternatives, so reading them is good practice.

answers.body: Combining several patterns in one model, for example a Singleton that is also a composite node.
answers.comment: L5, slide 28: Patterns are often combined, for example Singleton and Composite in the Model class.

name: Which statements about the essential elements of a pattern description are correct?

answers.body: The solution describes elements, relationships, responsibilities and collaborations, but never a specific concrete implementation.
answers.comment: L5, slide 9: Sample code is a separate, illustrative part of a pattern description.

answers.body: The consequences describe results and trade-offs, including the impact on flexibility, extensibility and portability.
answers.comment: L5, slide 9: They are critical for evaluating alternatives and understanding costs and benefits.

answers.body: The problem statement tells when to apply the pattern and explains the problem and its context, often with an example.
answers.comment: L5, slide 9: It is the "when" part of the description.

answers.body: The solution contains the exact source code that has to be used in every application of the pattern.
answers.comment: L5, slides 8-9: The solution does not prescribe a concrete implementation.

answers.body: The problem statement lists the results and trade-offs, while the consequences explain when to apply the pattern.
answers.comment: L5, slide 9: The two are swapped: the problem statement says when to apply, the consequences list the trade-offs.

name: GoF patterns are classified by purpose into creational, structural and behavioral. Which of the following are structural patterns?

answers.body: Adapter: it translates a "server" interface to the interface of our client code.
answers.comment: L5, slide 12: Structural patterns decouple interface and implementation and compose classes or objects.

answers.body: Flyweight: it lets many fine-grained objects be shared efficiently.
answers.comment: L5, slide 12: It is listed with the structural patterns, since it is about how objects are composed and shared.

answers.body: Builder: it builds a structure of objects that are connected to each other, so it is structural.
answers.comment: L5, slide 11: Builder is creational; it deals with creating and configuring objects incrementally.

answers.body: Iterator: it accesses the elements of a collection, so it is a structural pattern.
answers.comment: L5, slide 13: Iterator is behavioral; behavioral patterns deal with dynamic interactions among objects.

answers.body: Observer: it connects objects together in a fixed hierarchy of parts and wholes.
answers.comment: L5, slide 14: Observer is behavioral; dependents are updated automatically when the subject changes.

name: Which short characterizations of GoF patterns are correct?

answers.body: Builder: a factory for building complex objects incrementally.
answers.comment: L5, slide 11: A creational pattern that assembles a complex object step by step.

answers.body: Chain of Responsibility: a request is delegated to the responsible service provider.
answers.comment: L5, slide 13: A behavioral pattern that passes a request along until a provider handles it.

answers.body: Mediator: stores and recovers the state of an object.
answers.comment: L5, slide 13: That is Memento; Mediator coordinates interactions between its associates.

answers.body: Facade: extends an object transparently with new responsibilities.
answers.comment: L5, slide 12: That is Decorator; Facade simplifies and aggregates the interface of a complex subsystem.

answers.body: Prototype: a method in a derived class creates the associated objects.
answers.comment: L5, slide 11: That is Factory Method; Prototype creates new objects by cloning a prototype.

name: Patterns are also organized by scope: class scope versus object scope. A team wants to reuse a collection of collaborating objects by changing how they are composed at run time rather than by creating a new subclass for each variant. Which statements are correct?

answers.body: This is the object-scope approach: object-scope patterns (e.g. Composite, Decorator) relate peer objects and reuse by varying composition.
answers.comment: L5, slide 15: Object scope favors composition over sub-classing.

answers.body: Class-scope patterns (e.g. Factory Method, Template Method) fix the relations between a base class and all of its subclasses, as static semantics.
answers.comment: L5, slide 15: Class scope concerns inheritance relations that are decided at design time.

answers.body: This is a class-scope situation; the relationships between peer objects are static semantics fixed at design time.
answers.comment: L5, slide 15: Peer-object relationships are object scope; class scope concerns base classes and subclasses.

answers.body: Adapter belongs to the class scope only, so it can never be realized by composition with an associated adaptee object.
answers.comment: L5, slide 15: Adapter is listed in both scopes, as a class adapter and as an object adapter.

name: A chemistry application models a ChemStructure containing 1..* Molecules, each Molecule containing 1..* Residues, and each Residue containing 1..* Atoms. Atoms are reachable from their residue, residues from their molecule, and molecules from their chemical structure. Which statements are correct?

answers.body: Every object in a running OO system must be referenced: each class is associated with another class, or a few instances have well-known access points.
answers.comment: L5, slide 19: This is the access rule used to find the weak point of the model.

answers.body: Nothing references the (possibly multiple) chemical structures, so a Singleton Model class with <TT>instance()</TT> supplies the missing access point.
answers.comment: L5, slides 19-20, 23: The sole Model instance gives clients a pointer to a concrete chemical structure.

answers.body: Each Atom should keep a global static list of all ChemStructure objects so that any atom can serve as the access point.
answers.comment: L5, slides 19-23: The access point is one dedicated sole instance; scattering global state is criticized.

answers.body: A chemical structure can be reached from any atom by following the containment associations upward, so no access point is needed.
answers.comment: L5, slide 19: The associations lead from the whole to its parts; nothing leads to the top-level structures.

name:
public class Singleton {
  private static Singleton uniqueInstance;
  public static Singleton instance() {
    if (uniqueInstance == null) { uniqueInstance = new Singleton(); }
    return uniqueInstance;
  }
  public void operation1() { ... }
}
Which statements about this lazy Singleton and its required elements are correct?

answers.body: The static attribute <TT>uniqueInstance</TT> holds the sole instance; <TT>instance()</TT> creates it on the first call and returns it afterwards.
answers.comment: L5, slide 20: The first call creates the instance in memory; later calls reuse it.

answers.body: The constructor must be non-public (protected), so clients cannot create further instances with <TT>new</TT> and must use <TT>instance()</TT>.
answers.comment: L5, slide 20: The slide marks the protected constructor as a necessary element of the pattern.

answers.body: A public constructor is needed so that every client can obtain its own copy of the object whenever necessary.
answers.comment: L5, slide 20: Clients use instance(); a public constructor would allow additional instances.

answers.body: <TT>operation1()</TT> and <TT>operation2()</TT> have to be static methods, so that no instance of the class is ever created.
answers.comment: L5, slides 20-21: The operations are ordinary instance methods invoked on the sole instance; static operations are less flexible.

name: Instead of a Singleton, one could simply put all operations into a class as static (class) operations. Which are advantages of the Singleton over this solution?

answers.body: The Singleton class may be subclassed, and the application can be configured with an instance of any extended class at run time.
answers.comment: L5, slide 21: Instance methods can be overridden, so the sole instance can be of a subclass.

answers.body: It permits a variable number of instances later, which is hard to change when everything is static.
answers.comment: L5, slide 21: The design can be changed to allow more than one instance of the class.

answers.body: Static operations are virtual, so subclasses can override them polymorphically; the Singleton adds nothing here.
answers.comment: L5, slide 21: Static functions are never virtual, so subclasses cannot override them polymorphically.

answers.body: A Singleton makes unit tests fully independent of each other; it carries no state between tests.
answers.comment: L5, slide 22: The opposite holds: singletons carry state for the application lifetime, so tests may need ordering.

answers.body: A Singleton removes the need for a well-known access point; every class can create it on demand.
answers.comment: L5, slides 20-21: A Singleton offers a well-known access point (instance()); it does not remove the need for one.

name: Why do some designers consider the Singleton an anti-pattern?

answers.body: It introduces global state, and making something global just to avoid passing it around is never harmless: a code smell.
answers.comment: L5, slide 22: Global state hides dependencies.

answers.body: It violates single responsibility, because it also controls its own creation and life cycle.
answers.comment: L5, slide 22: Creation and life-cycle control is a second responsibility.

answers.body: It cannot be subclassed, so the application can never be configured with an extended version of the class.
answers.comment: L5, slide 21: The Singleton class may be subclassed; this is listed as an advantage.

answers.body: It avoids concurrency problems.
answers.comment: L5, slide 22: Concurrency problems are named as one of the criticisms.

answers.body: The recommended remedy is to replace the Singleton by a larger set of static utility methods in a helper class.
answers.comment: L5, slides 21-22: Static operations are less flexible; the slide suggests dependency injection and ORM of modern frameworks.

name: Which statements about the Composite pattern are correct?

answers.body: Component declares a generic interface (operation, add, remove, getChild) for any tree node; Composite forwards operation() to all children.
answers.comment: L5, slide 26: Leaves and composites are treated through the same interface; a Component is usually not instantiated.

answers.body: It makes adding new node kinds easy (open-closed), but the design becomes overly general and restricting a composite's components is harder.
answers.comment: L5, slide 27: These are the stated consequences.

answers.body: Clients have to check whether a node is a leaf or a composite before they call operation() on it; the interfaces differ.
answers.comment: L5, slide 27: Clients ignore the difference and treat all objects uniformly.

answers.body: A Leaf also keeps a list of children for later use, but it never forwards operation() to them when it is invoked.
answers.comment: L5, slide 26: A Leaf is a primitive node without children; only the Composite holds children and forwards the operation.

name: A Composite hierarchy has two kinds of composites (Composite1, Composite2) and two kinds of leaves (Leaf1, Leaf2). In variant A an abstract Composite superclass holds add, remove, getChild and the children association for both composites, and an abstract Leaf superclass is shared by both leaves. In variant B every concrete class inherits directly from Component and implements its child handling itself. Which statements are correct?

answers.body: For composites variant A is strongly recommended; differently stored children can still be handled by overriding in the subclasses.
answers.comment: L5, slide 29: The common supertype removes duplicated child management.

answers.body: For leaves variant A is preferred even if the leaves share nothing now, since they may later share a method, and clients can test the Leaf type.
answers.comment: L5, slide 30: A shared Leaf type allows future auto-propagating methods and a simple leaf check.

answers.body: Variant B is preferred for composites; duplicating the child management in each class keeps the classes independent.
answers.comment: L5, slides 25, 29: Duplicated code is what the generalization removes; independence is not a goal here.

answers.body: For leaves, a common supertype is pointless unless the leaves already share code today; otherwise the hierarchy is noise.
answers.comment: L5, slide 30: Even without current shared code, leaves may share something in the future, and the type enables a leaf check.

answers.body: A common Composite supertype is impossible when the two composites store their children in different ways.
answers.comment: L5, slide 29: Different storage can still be handled by overriding the behavior in the subclasses.

name: Which statements about the Iterator pattern are correct?

answers.body: <TT>Aggregate</TT> declares <TT>createIterator()</TT>; <TT>ConcreteAggregate</TT> returns <TT>new ConcreteIterator(this)</TT>, so the iterator links back to its aggregate.
answers.comment: L5, slides 35-36: The iterator is created by the aggregate and keeps a reference to it.

answers.body: A traversal is a loop: while <TT>hasNext()</TT> the client calls <TT>current()</TT> and <TT>next()</TT>, until all elements are visited; <TT>first()</TT> restarts it.
answers.comment: L5, slides 35-36: This is the protocol shown in the sequence diagram.

answers.body: The Aggregate interface additionally offers a <TT>getItem(i)</TT> method so that clients can read elements directly.
answers.comment: L5, slide 35: The slide notes that there is no getItem()-like method; access goes through the iterator.

answers.body: Only one traversal of an aggregate can be pending at a time; the aggregate itself stores the current traversal position.
answers.comment: L5, slide 37: The iterator keeps the position, so more than one traversal can be pending on an aggregate.

answers.body: The client creates the iterator itself with <TT>new ConcreteIterator()</TT> and passes the aggregate afterwards.
answers.comment: L5, slides 35-36: The aggregate creates the iterator via createIterator(), hiding its concrete class.

name: A <TT>Line</TT> class in a public transport system offers <TT>getWorkdays() : [Stop]</TT> and <TT>getWeekends() : [Stop]</TT>. It is redesigned so that the aggregate Line offers <TT>getIterator(dayType)</TT>, which instantiates a <TT>TimetableIterator</TT> with the subclasses <TT>WorkdayIterator</TT> and <TT>WeekendIterator</TT>. Which statements are correct?

answers.body: A new kind of day needs only a new iterator subclass and no change of Line, which is the open-closed principle.
answers.comment: L5, slide 40: The redesign supports multiple variations of the traversal.

answers.body: The Line interface gets simpler, because one operation replaces a getter per day type (single responsibility).
answers.comment: L5, slides 37, 40: Iterators simplify the Aggregate interface.

answers.body: Clients can reach the stops only if Line exposes its internal collection, for example as a public array.
answers.comment: L5, slide 37: Iterators give access to the contents without exposing the internal representation.

answers.body: Every aggregation in a model should get its own iterator class, even when a standard collection would do.
answers.comment: L5, slide 41: Standard collections with their iterators can be used for most cases.

answers.body: Each composite or aggregate class needs its own dedicated iterator class.
answers.comment: L5, slide 38: One iterator can be shared by multiple composites.

name: Which pairs of a Java core API element and the design pattern it exemplifies are correct?

answers.body: <TT>java.lang.Runtime#getRuntime()</TT> returns the runtime object of the application: Singleton.
answers.comment: L5, slide 24: A static accessor returns the sole instance.

answers.body: <TT>java.util.Collection#iterator()</TT> and the for-each loop traverse elements: Iterator.
answers.comment: L5, slide 39: Iterators are integrated into the syntax of most OO languages as for-each loops.

answers.body: <TT>java.awt.Container#add(Component)</TT> appends a component to the container: Singleton.
answers.comment: L5, slide 31: A container that holds components, which may be containers themselves, is a Composite.

answers.body: <TT>java.awt.Desktop#getDesktop()</TT> returns the desktop of the browser context: Composite.
answers.comment: L5, slide 24: It returns the desktop instance of the current browser context, which is a Singleton.

answers.body: <TT>java.util.Collection#iterator()</TT> returns an iterator over the elements: Composite.
answers.comment: L5, slide 39: The method returns an Iterator for traversing the elements, not a part-whole tree.

name: In the chemistry model the sole <TT>Model</TT> instance manages ChemStructures, which contain Molecules, Residues and Atoms. Which statements about combining patterns in such a model are correct?

answers.body: Patterns are often combined: the Model class can be a Singleton and, at the same time, a composite node of the Composite tree.
answers.comment: L5, slide 28: Model carries both stereotypes.

answers.body: The composite classes can also play the aggregate role of Iterator and offer <TT>createIterator()</TT>, which hides how all children are stored.
answers.comment: L5, slides 34, 38: Composite nodes are thought of as containers of their children.

answers.body: A class may play a role in only one pattern at a time, so Model has to choose between Singleton and Composite.
answers.comment: L5, slides 28, 38: Model plays several roles at once (singleton, composite, iterator aggregate).

answers.body: When <TT>setColor()</TT> is called on a group element, only the group itself changes color and its children keep theirs.
answers.comment: L5, slide 28: The operation is applied to all children of the group.

name: Practical modeling: a chemistry application has the classes Model (a Singleton with instance() and loadChemStructure(File)), ChemStructure, Molecule, Residue and Atom. Each of the first four has its own nearly identical methods addX/removeX/getX(int) for the next level (ChemStructure manages molecules, Molecule residues, Residue atoms), and each level contains 1..* objects of the next. Redesign the model with the Composite pattern in a UML class diagram, add an operation setColor(Color) that colours a whole subtree, and explain which roles the classes play and what the redesign improves. Then explain how you would hide how the children are stored and allow different traversals.
answer: The model is a tree of objects, so the classes can be generalized to a parent-child abstraction. Introduce an abstract <<composite-component>> ModelElement with add(ModelElement), remove(ModelElement), get(int): ModelElement and setColor(Color). <<composite-leaf>> Atom inherits from ModelElement and keeps its color attribute; setColor() sets it. <<composite-composite>> GroupElement inherits from ModelElement, holds the subElements association (1..* ModelElement, with superElement as the opposite end), implements add/remove/get and implements setColor() by applying it to all children. Molecule, Residue, ChemStructure and Model become subclasses of GroupElement; Model additionally stays a <<singleton>> with instance() and loadChemStructure(File) – patterns are often combined. Improvements: the duplicated addX/removeX/getX methods are replaced by unified methods, clients treat atoms and groups uniformly, and new kinds of nodes are easy to add (open-closed principle); the trade-off is a more general design that makes it harder to restrict which children a node may have (e.g. that a Residue contains only Atoms). To hide the representation of children and support various traversals, think of composite nodes as containers and apply Iterator: the composites (aggregates) offer createIterator(): Iterator, the subElements attribute can move to the individual subclasses so each can store children differently, and iterator classes such as ResidueIterator or ChemStructureIterator are instantiated by the composites; one iterator can be shared by several composites.
keyPoints: Abstract component ModelElement with add, remove, get(int), setColor
Atom = leaf; GroupElement = composite with subElements 1..* and superElement
Molecule, Residue, ChemStructure, Model inherit from GroupElement; Model also Singleton
GroupElement.setColor applies setColor to all children
Benefits: no duplicated methods, uniform treatment, easy extension (OCP); cost: harder to restrict children
Iterator: composites as aggregates with createIterator(); iterators can be shared

name: Practical modeling: a public transport company models a city plan. A CityPlan contains Lines; a Line has Stops and a LineNumber; ConstructionSigns can be attached either to a Line or to a Stop (exclusively). There are TramLines, BusLines and TrolleyBusLines. A first model uses a separate dedicated association for every pair of classes. Explain why this model is weak when a new kind of element (for example another type of sign) must be added. Then redesign it with the Composite pattern so that every element of the plan can be highlighted with highlight(), and state which single class of your redesigned model is a candidate for the Singleton pattern and why.
answer: The objects of the city plan form a tree: CityPlan → Line → Stop/LineNumber, with ConstructionSigns under a Line or a Stop. With a dedicated association for every pair (CityPlan–Line, Line–Stop, Line–LineNumber, Line or Stop–ConstructionSign with an {XOR} constraint), every new kind of element (e.g. another type of sign) requires new associations and new methods in the classes that contain it – the extensibility and maintainability of the model is weak. Composite redesign: an abstract CityPlanElement (component) with highlight(); an abstract Leaf and an abstract Composite inherit from it, the Composite holding the children association (* CityPlanElement) and implementing highlight() for all children. ConstructionSign and LineNumber are leaves (ConstructionSign placed under a Line or a Stop, LineNumber under a Line); CityPlan, Line and Stop are composites (Line under CityPlan, Stop under Line). The CityPlan is the root of the tree (there is one plan that clients must reach through a well-known access point), so it is the candidate for the Singleton pattern. A new kind of element (e.g. another sign type) then becomes just another Leaf subclass. Trade-off: the generic children association no longer enforces which elements may be placed where, so these rules must be checked elsewhere.
keyPoints: Model is a tree of objects; pairwise associations make every new element costly (weak extensibility)
CityPlanElement component with highlight()
Abstract Leaf and Composite; Composite holds children and propagates highlight()
Leaves: ConstructionSign (under Line or Stop), LineNumber (under Line); composites: CityPlan, Line, Stop
CityPlan = root, candidate for Singleton
New element = new leaf; placement rules no longer enforced by associations

name: A music app stores songs in <TT>Playlist</TT> as an array and offers <TT>getSong(int i)</TT> and <TT>size()</TT>. Clients write index loops over this array. The team also wants to traverse a playlist in reverse order and to hide the way the songs are stored (array today, linked list later). Redesign the class model with the Iterator pattern: draw a UML class diagram with the pattern roles, describe a traversal as a sequence of calls, and explain which SOLID principles the redesign supports. (The scenario is derived; the pattern structure is from the lecture.)
answer:
Class diagram. The playlist becomes the aggregate: interface <<aggregate>> Playlist with createIterator() : Iterator, and ConcretePlaylist (holding the songs in its array) which returns new ConcreteIterator(this), so the iterator gets a link to its originating playlist. The interface <<iterator>> Iterator has first(), next(), hasNext() : boolean and current() : Song. ForwardIterator and ReverseIterator specialize it and are instantiated by the playlist. The aggregate has no getSong(i)-like method any more; elements are reached through the iterator. The client depends only on Playlist and Iterator, with Song as the item (0..* songs in the aggregate).
Traversal. The client calls createIterator(); the playlist creates the iterator with a reference to itself. Then the client loops: while hasNext() it calls current() (the iterator inspects the playlist) and next(). At the end the iterator is destroyed. Several iterators can be pending on one playlist at the same time.
Principles. Open-closed: a new traversal order is a new iterator subclass, and Playlist is unchanged. Single responsibility: iterators simplify the aggregate interface because traversal logic lives outside it. Hiding the representation means that replacing the array by a linked list changes only the iterator class and the playlist, not the clients. Standard library collections with their iterators suffice in many cases, so a custom iterator is only worth it for special traversals.
keyPoints: Aggregate with createIterator() and a concrete aggregate returning new ConcreteIterator(this)
Iterator interface with first, next, hasNext, current; forward and reverse iterator subclasses
No getSong(i)-like access method on the aggregate; clients use only Playlist and Iterator
Traversal: createIterator, then loop hasNext / current / next; several traversals may be pending
Open-closed (new traversal = new iterator) and single responsibility (simpler aggregate); representation stays hidden

name: A small program needs a configuration registry that every part of the system reaches through one well-known access point and of which exactly one object may exist. Model it with the Singleton pattern: draw the UML class with its members, write the Java code of the access method and constructor, and explain what the pattern gives you compared with static operations. Then name two criticisms of the pattern and the alternative that the lecture suggests. (The registry scenario is derived; the pattern is from the lecture.)
answer:
Class. Class ConfigRegistry (stereotype <<singleton>>) with the private static attribute uniqueInstance : ConfigRegistry, the public static (underlined) operation instance() : ConfigRegistry, a protected constructor, and ordinary instance operations such as get(key) and set(key, value).
public class ConfigRegistry {
  private static ConfigRegistry uniqueInstance;
  protected ConfigRegistry() { }
  public static ConfigRegistry instance() {
    if (uniqueInstance == null) {
      uniqueInstance = new ConfigRegistry();
    }
    return uniqueInstance;
  }
  public String get(String key) { ... }
}
Clients write ConfigRegistry.instance().get("url"); the first call creates the object, later calls reuse it.
Versus static operations. Access to the sole instance is controlled; the class may be subclassed and configured at run time with an instance of the extended class; the number of instances can later become variable; and instance methods can be overridden, while static functions are never virtual.
Criticisms. (1) It introduces global state, a code smell, and carries state for the whole application lifetime, which makes tests depend on each other and need an order. (2) It violates single responsibility, because it controls its own creation and life cycle, and it causes concurrency problems.
Alternative. Use dependency injection and ORM of modern frameworks (e.g. Spring) instead of a hand-written Singleton.
keyPoints: Singleton class with private static uniqueInstance, public static instance(), protected constructor
Lazy creation: first call creates the object, later calls return the same one
Benefits over static operations: controlled access, subclassing and run-time configuration, variable number of instances, overridable methods
Criticisms: global state, hard-to-order tests, single responsibility violation, concurrency
Lecture suggests dependency injection and frameworks (e.g. Spring) as the alternative
source: L5, slides 20-22; the registry scenario is derived
